C005.subject: The specific fractal dimension of the basin boundary in T(n)
C005.object: the critical perturbation threshold below which cycle stability is preserved, thereby constraining the topology of evolutionary fitness landscapes
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The specific fractal dimension of the basin boundary in T(n) the critical perturbation threshold below which cycle stability is preserved, thereby constraining the topology of evolutionary fitness landscapes]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic numerical estimation of the fractal dimension of basin boundaries in T(n) across varying perturbation amplitudes, using box-counting or correlation dimension methods, and comparing these to the observed critical perturbation threshold below which cycles remain stable. — Directly tests the hypothesized modulation by measuring both the fractal dimension and the threshold in the same simulation runs, allowing for a correlational or causal test of the relationship.

[PATH:theoretical] Analytical derivation of the relationship between basin boundary fractal dimension and the stability radius of attractors in discrete-time dynamical systems, building on existing theory (e.g., Grebogi et al., 1983; McDonald et al., 1985) and extending it to the specific structure of T(n). — Provides a formal mathematical foundation that could confirm or refute whether fractal dimension necessarily constrains the perturbation threshold, independent of simulation-specific parameters.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published computational evolutionary dynamics studies that report basin boundary structures and perturbation thresholds in T(n) or similar systems (e.g., fitness landscape models, NK landscapes, or genotype-phenotype maps), extracting relevant data to test for a consistent relationship. — Leverages existing evidence to assess the generality of the hypothesis across different parameter ranges and model variants, potentially refuting it if no consistent modulation is found.

qualifier.temporal: during simulation runs of T(n) under default parameter ranges

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Initial condition variations in T(n) the stability of cycles, as evolutionary fitness landscapes are primarily influenced by external factors]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic perturbation experiments on T(n) initial conditions in neutral spatial evolutionary simulations, measuring cycle stability metrics (e.g., period, amplitude, attractor basin size) over 10^4 generations and comparing to simulations with controlled external factor variations (e.g., mutation rate, selection pressure). — Directly tests the claim by manipulating initial conditions while controlling for external factors; if cycle stability varies with initial conditions despite constant external landscape, the hypothesis is refuted.

[PATH:theoretical] Analytical derivation of stability conditions for evolutionary cycles in neutral spatial models, using dynamical systems theory to map the influence of initial T(n) values on attractor structure versus the influence of external parameters (e.g., interaction range, reproduction rate). — Provides a formal, generalizable understanding of whether initial conditions can affect stability independently of external factors, complementing empirical tests with causal logic.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published computational evolutionary dynamics studies (e.g., from journals like PLoS Computational Biology, Evolution) that report cycle stability under varying initial conditions and external factors in neutral spatial settings, focusing on the first 10^4 generations. — Aggregates existing evidence to assess the weight of support for the hypothesis across multiple models and parameter regimes, identifying consensus or contradictions.

qualifier.temporal: within the first 10^4 generations of simulation
qualifier.geographic: in silico, under neutral spatial structure

[PATH:literature] Review of known results on the dynamics of related Collatz-type functions, particularly studies of period lengths and basin sizes in generalized 3x+1 problems — Contextualizes the hypothesis within existing literature, revealing whether similar number-theoretic properties have been shown to determine basin structure in analogous recursions, thus indicating plausibility or providing refuting examples.
